Five and Seven simply looked at Two without replying. In a low voice, Two began, “Well, you see, Miss, the thing is, this was supposed to be a _red_ rose-tree. We planted a white one by mistake. If the Queen finds out, we’ll all lose our heads, you know. So we’re doing our best, Miss, before she comes, to—” At that instant Five, who had been anxiously watching the garden, shouted, “The Queen! The Queen!” All three gardeners immediately fell flat on their faces. Many footsteps approached, and Alice turned eagerly to see the Queen.

First came ten soldiers carrying clubs. Like the gardeners, they were flat and oblong, with hands and feet at their corners. Ten courtiers followed, covered in diamonds and walking in pairs, just as the soldiers did. Next came the royal children, ten little dears skipping happily along hand in hand, two by two, all decorated with hearts. Then came the guests, chiefly Kings and Queens. Among them Alice recognised the White Rabbit, talking nervously and hurriedly and smiling at everything anyone said; he passed without noticing her. After them came the Knave of Hearts, bearing the King’s crown on a crimson velvet cushion. Finally, at the end of this magnificent procession, came THE KING AND QUEEN OF HEARTS.

Alice wondered whether she should lie facedown like the gardeners, but she could not remember hearing of any such rule for processions. “Besides,” she thought, “what would be the point of a procession if everybody had to lie on their faces and couldn’t see it?” She stayed where she was and waited.
When the procession reached Alice, everyone stopped to stare. “Who is this?” the Queen asked sternly. The question was addressed to the Knave of Hearts, whose only answer was a bow and a smile.
“Idiot!” the Queen said, tossing her head impatiently. Then she turned to Alice. “Child, what is your name?”
“My name is Alice, your Majesty, if you please,” Alice replied with great politeness. But to herself she added, “After all, they’re just a pack of cards. There’s no need to be frightened!”

“And who are _these?_” the Queen asked, pointing to the three gardeners lying beside the rose-tree. You see, they were facedown, and the designs on their backs matched the rest of the pack. She could not tell whether they were gardeners, soldiers, courtiers, or even three of her own children.
“How would _I_ know?” Alice answered, amazed at her own boldness. “It’s none of _my_ business.”
The Queen’s face went crimson with rage. She stared at Alice like a wild animal for a moment, then screamed, “Off with her head! Off—”
“Nonsense!” Alice declared loudly and firmly. The Queen fell silent.
Putting his hand on her arm, the King ventured timidly, “Remember, my dear: she’s only a child!”
The Queen turned away from him angrily and ordered the Knave, “Turn them over!”
Using one foot, the Knave carefully did as she asked.
“Stand up!” the Queen commanded in a loud, piercing voice. The gardeners sprang up and bowed to the King, the Queen, the royal children, and everyone else.
“Stop that!” shrieked the Queen. “You’re making me dizzy.” Turning towards the rose-tree, she demanded, “What _have_ you been doing here?”
Two dropped to one knee. “If it please your Majesty,” he began very humbly, “we were trying to—”

“_I_ can see!” the Queen said, having meanwhile inspected the roses. “Off with their heads!” The procession continued, leaving three soldiers to execute the unlucky gardeners, who rushed to Alice for safety.
“You won’t lose your heads!” Alice assured them. She hid them in a large flowerpot nearby. The soldiers searched about for a minute or two, then quietly marched away to rejoin the others.
“Have their heads been cut off?” the Queen shouted.
The soldiers called back, “Their heads are gone, your Majesty, if you please!”
“Good!” the Queen shouted. “Do you know how to play croquet?”
The soldiers said nothing. They looked at Alice, since the Queen was clearly asking her.
Alice shouted, “Yes!”
“Then come along!” roared the Queen. Alice fell in with the procession, full of curiosity about what might happen next.
A timid voice beside her said, “It’s—it’s a lovely day!” The White Rabbit was walking next to her, peering anxiously into her face.
“Lovely,” Alice agreed. “—Where is the Duchess?”
“Hush! Hush!” the Rabbit said quickly and quietly, casting a nervous glance over his shoulder. He stood on tiptoe, brought his mouth to her ear, and whispered, “She’s been sentenced to death.”
Alice asked, “What for?”
“Was that ‘What a pity!’ you said?” asked the Rabbit.
“No,” Alice replied. “I don’t think it’s a pity at all. I asked, ‘What for?’”

“She boxed the Queen’s ears—” the Rabbit began. Alice let out a little shriek of laughter. “Oh, be quiet!” he whispered fearfully. “The Queen will hear! You see, she arrived rather late, and the Queen said—”

“Take your places!” the Queen thundered. Everyone began running in different directions and bumping into one another. After a minute or two, however, they settled into position and the game began. Alice had never seen such an extraordinary croquet-ground: ridges and furrows ran everywhere; living hedgehogs served as balls, living flamingoes as mallets, and the soldiers bent double, balancing on their hands and feet to form the arches.

At first Alice’s main problem was controlling her flamingo. She could tuck its body fairly comfortably beneath her arm, letting its legs dangle. But usually, just as she had straightened its neck and was about to strike the hedgehog with its head, it _insisted_ on twisting round and looking up at her with such a bewildered face that she burst out laughing. Once she lowered its head and tried again, she would discover, most annoyingly, that the hedgehog had uncurled and was crawling off. On top of all that, wherever she wanted to send the hedgehog, a ridge or furrow generally blocked the way. The bent-over soldiers kept standing up and strolling to other parts of the ground, too. Alice soon decided that this was an extremely difficult game indeed.

Everyone played at once, without taking turns, arguing constantly and struggling over the hedgehogs. Before long the Queen was in a terrible rage, stamping about and yelling “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!” roughly once a minute.

Alice grew increasingly uneasy. She had not quarrelled with the Queen herself yet, but it could happen at any moment. “And what would happen to me then?” she wondered. “They’re terribly keen on cutting off heads here. It’s amazing anyone is still alive!”

She was searching for an escape route, wondering whether she could leave unnoticed, when she saw something strange in the air. At first she could not work it out. After watching for a minute or two, though, she recognised a grin. “It’s the Cheshire Cat,” she thought. “Now I’ll have someone to talk to.”
As soon as enough of its mouth had appeared to speak, the Cat asked, “How are things going?”

Alice waited for its eyes to appear before nodding. “There’s no point speaking,” she thought, “until its ears arrive—or at least one of them.” Another minute brought the whole head into view. Alice put her flamingo down and began describing the game, delighted to have someone listening. Apparently the Cat thought enough of itself was visible now, because nothing more appeared.

“I don’t think they play fairly at all,” Alice began, sounding rather aggrieved. “They argue so much you can’t hear yourself speak, and there don’t seem to be any definite rules—or if there are, nobody follows them. And you can’t imagine how confusing it is when all the equipment is alive! The arch I’m supposed to go through next, for example, is wandering about at the far end of the ground. And just now I should have croqueted the Queen’s hedgehog, but it ran off when it saw mine approaching!”
Quietly, the Cat asked, “What do you think of the Queen?”

“I don’t like her at all,” Alice said. “She’s so terribly—” Then she noticed the Queen standing right behind her, listening. “—likely to win,” she continued, “that finishing the game hardly seems worthwhile.”
Smiling, the Queen moved on.
The King approached Alice and gazed at the Cat’s head with great interest. “Who _are_ you speaking to?” he asked.
“A friend of mine, a Cheshire Cat,” Alice answered. “May I introduce you?”
“I don’t care for its appearance at all,” the King said. “Still, it may kiss my hand if it wishes.”
The Cat replied, “I’d prefer not to.”
“Don’t be insolent,” the King said, moving behind Alice as he spoke. “And stop looking at me that way!”
“A cat may look at a king,” Alice said. “I read that somewhere in a book, though I can’t remember which.”
“Well, it will have to be removed,” the King declared firmly. As the Queen passed, he called, “My dear! Please have this cat taken away!”
The Queen dealt with every difficulty, large or small, in the same way. Without even turning her head, she ordered, “Off with his head!”
“I’ll get the executioner myself,” the King said eagerly, hurrying away.

Hearing the Queen screaming furiously in the distance, Alice decided she might as well return and see how the game was going. Already the Queen had condemned three players to death for missing their turns. Alice felt very unhappy about this, since the game was so chaotic that she could never tell whether it was her turn. She went to look for her hedgehog.

It was fighting another hedgehog. Alice thought this offered an excellent chance to croquet one with the other. The only problem was that her flamingo had wandered to the other side of the garden, where she could see it making helpless attempts to fly into a tree.

By the time she caught the flamingo and returned, the fight had ended and both hedgehogs had disappeared. “But it hardly matters,” Alice thought. “There aren’t any arches left on this side of the ground anyway.” She tucked the flamingo under her arm to prevent another escape and went back to talk some more with her friend.

On returning to the Cheshire Cat, Alice was surprised to discover that quite a large crowd had gathered around it. A dispute was under way between the executioner, the King, and the Queen, all speaking together. Everyone else stood in complete silence and looked deeply uncomfortable.

The instant they saw Alice, all three asked her to settle their dispute. They repeated their arguments, but since they spoke over one another, she could scarcely make out exactly what anyone was saying.
The executioner argued that you could not cut a head off without a body to cut it off from. He had never been asked to do such a thing before, and he certainly would not start at _his_ age.
The King argued that anything with a head could have its head cut off, and people should stop talking nonsense.
The Queen argued that unless something was done about it in less than no time, she would have everyone there executed. (That last remark was what had made the whole group look so solemn and worried.)
All Alice could think to say was, “The Cat belongs to the Duchess. You’d better ask _her_.”
“She’s in prison,” the Queen told the executioner. “Bring her here.” He shot away like an arrow.

The moment he left, the Cat’s head began to fade. By the time he returned with the Duchess, it had vanished completely. The King and executioner rushed frantically up and down looking for it, while everyone else returned to the game.
